p: Today it was very hot. We went to the beach to cool down. I wore my hat and put on sunscreen.
It rained all day on Monday. The water made big puddles. I jumped in them with my red boots.

p: Australia is a large country with many different climates. The north is tropical, with a wet season and a dry season. The south has four seasons, with hot summers and cool winters. The centre is mostly desert, where it can be very hot during the day and cold at night.

The sun in Australia is very strong, so it is important to protect your skin. Remember to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, seek shade and slide on sunglasses. Doing this every day, even when it is cloudy, can help prevent skin cancer.

A cyclone is a powerful storm that forms over warm ocean water. It has very strong winds that spin around a calm centre called the eye. Cyclones can damage buildings, knock down trees and cause flooding. People in northern Australia prepare emergency kits before each cyclone season.

Our class made a weather station in the playground. We used a thermometer to measure the temperature, a rain gauge to collect rain and a windsock to show the wind direction. Each morning we recorded the results and made a graph at the end of the month.

During a drought, there is much less rain than usual for a long time. Rivers and dams dry up, and the ground becomes hard and cracked. Farmers may have to buy food and water for their animals. Everyone can help by saving water at home.

When there is a storm, it is safest to stay indoors. Lightning can strike tall objects such as trees and poles, so you should never shelter under them. Count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder. The shorter the gap, the closer the storm is to you.

s: Weather describes conditions over a short period, while climate refers to patterns measured over many years.
El Nino events are often linked to drier conditions across eastern Australia.
Bushfire danger ratings help communities understand how dangerous fire conditions are on a given day.
Australia's position in the Southern Hemisphere means its seasons are opposite to those in Europe.
Humidity measures how much water vapour is in the air, which affects how hot it feels.
Cold fronts moving up from the Southern Ocean bring wind, rain and lower temperatures.
Meteorologists use computer models to predict how air pressure systems will move.
Heatwaves cause more deaths in Australia than any other type of natural hazard.
Floodwater can be deceptive, hiding debris, strong currents and damaged roads beneath its surface.
Urban areas are often hotter than the surrounding countryside because concrete absorbs and stores heat.
The monsoon brings heavy rainfall to northern Australia between December and March.
Thunderstorm asthma can occur when storms break pollen into tiny particles that people breathe in.
Fog forms when air near the ground cools to the point where water vapour condenses.
The Bureau of Meteorology has collected weather records in Australia for more than a century.
Rain shadows occur on the side of a mountain range that is sheltered from moist winds.
Tropical cyclones are given names so that warnings are easier to communicate to the public.
Planting trees in streets can lower local temperatures by providing shade and releasing moisture.
A barometer measures air pressure, and falling pressure often signals approaching bad weather.
Snowfall in the Australian Alps varies greatly from year to year.
Lightning strikes start many bushfires in remote parts of the country.
Water restrictions limit when gardens can be watered during long periods of drought.
Sea breezes form on summer afternoons when land heats faster than the ocean.
Weather balloons carry instruments high into the atmosphere to measure temperature and wind.
Emergency services encourage families to prepare a written plan for floods, storms and bushfires.
Seasonal knowledge held by Aboriginal peoples recognises six or more seasons in some regions.
p: Weather and climate are related but different. Weather describes the conditions we experience on a particular day, such as rain, wind and temperature. Climate is the average pattern of weather in a place over a long period, usually thirty years or more. For example, Darwin has a tropical climate, even though some days there may be mild and dry.

Heatwaves are one of Australia's most dangerous natural hazards. During extended periods of extreme heat, the elderly, young children and people with health conditions are most at risk. Staying hydrated, avoiding strenuous activity in the middle of the day and checking on vulnerable neighbours can save lives. Cities are also adding shade and cool spaces to help residents cope.

The El Nino Southern Oscillation is a climate pattern involving changes in ocean temperatures across the Pacific. During El Nino years, eastern Australia often experiences warmer and drier conditions, increasing the risk of drought and bushfire. During La Nina years, the opposite usually happens, with more rain and flooding. Forecasters monitor the Pacific closely to predict these patterns months ahead.

Many Aboriginal communities recognise seasons that are closely tied to local plants and animals rather than calendar months. In parts of northern Australia, people describe six distinct seasons, marked by changes such as the flowering of certain trees or the arrival of particular birds. This knowledge, developed over thousands of years, offers a detailed understanding of the local environment.

Bushfires are a natural part of the Australian landscape, but hot, dry and windy conditions can make them extremely dangerous. The Australian Fire Danger Rating System uses four levels, from moderate to catastrophic, to help people decide what action to take. On the highest-rated days, the safest option is usually to leave high-risk areas early rather than wait.

Floods can develop slowly over several days or arrive suddenly after intense rain. Flash floods are particularly dangerous because they give little warning. Just fifteen centimetres of fast-flowing water can knock an adult over, and sixty centimetres can float a car. That is why emergency services repeatedly warn people never to walk, swim or drive through floodwater.

s: Australia's climate is highly variable, shaped by interactions between the Pacific, Indian and Southern Oceans.
Climate scientists project that extreme heat events will become more frequent and intense as global temperatures rise.
The Indian Ocean Dipole can strongly influence rainfall across southern and eastern Australia during winter and spring.
Attribution science allows researchers to estimate how much climate change has increased the likelihood of a specific event.
The Black Summer bushfires of 2019 and 2020 burned an area larger than many countries.
Improved forecasting has reduced deaths from tropical cyclones, although damage to property continues to rise.
Rising sea levels increase the risk of coastal flooding during storm surges and king tides.
Urban heat islands can be mitigated through cool roofs, green spaces and better building design.
Compound events, such as drought followed by fire and flood, place enormous strain on communities and services.
Insurance premiums in flood-prone areas have risen sharply, raising questions about where people should live.
The Southern Annular Mode influences the position of westerly winds and the rainfall they bring.
Long-term rainfall decline in south-west Western Australia has had major consequences for water supply.
Ocean warming contributes to more intense rainfall because warmer air can hold more moisture.
Early warning systems rely on accurate data, clear communication and public trust to be effective.
Some scientists argue that the traditional four seasons poorly describe Australia's diverse regional climates.
Paleoclimate records from tree rings and ice cores reveal how climate varied long before instruments existed.
Adaptation strategies, including drought-resistant crops and flood-resilient housing, are becoming increasingly important.
The economic cost of natural disasters in Australia is expected to grow substantially in coming decades.
Heat-related illness can be prevented through public education, cooling centres and changes to work practices.
Weather radar networks detect precipitation and wind patterns, helping forecasters issue timely warnings.
Snow cover in the Australian Alps has declined over recent decades, affecting both ecosystems and tourism.
The relationship between climate change and bushfire risk involves temperature, fuel dryness and fire weather.
Effective climate communication must balance scientific uncertainty with the urgency of the risks involved.
Indigenous seasonal calendars are increasingly recognised as valuable records of environmental change.
Resilient infrastructure must be designed for the climate of the future rather than the climate of the past.
p: Australia experiences some of the most variable rainfall in the world. Major climate drivers, including the El Nino Southern Oscillation, the Indian Ocean Dipole and the Southern Annular Mode, interact in complex ways to determine whether a season will be wet or dry. This variability has always challenged farmers and water managers. Climate change adds another layer of complexity, altering the background conditions in which these natural patterns operate and influencing the severity of droughts and floods.

The Black Summer bushfires of 2019 and 2020 were among the most destructive in Australian history. Fires burned through millions of hectares, destroyed thousands of homes and killed or displaced an estimated three billion animals. Smoke affected air quality in major cities for weeks. A subsequent royal commission found that extreme fire weather had become more common and recommended improvements in national coordination, emergency warnings and the use of traditional land management practices.

Urban heat islands form when natural landscapes are replaced by roads, roofs and other surfaces that absorb and retain heat. In some western Sydney suburbs, summer temperatures can be several degrees higher than in coastal areas. Planners are responding by increasing tree canopy, using lighter coloured roofing materials and creating water features in public spaces. These strategies not only reduce temperatures but also lower energy demand and improve public health during heatwaves.

Extreme weather attribution is a relatively new field of climate science. By comparing climate models that include human greenhouse gas emissions with models that do not, researchers can estimate how much more likely or intense a particular heatwave, flood or drought has become. These studies help communicate the real-world consequences of climate change. However, scientists stress that results depend on the quality of data and models, and that some events are more easily attributed than others.

Rising sea levels pose a long-term threat to coastal communities around Australia, where a large proportion of the population lives. As oceans warm and ice sheets melt, higher water levels increase the impact of storm surges and erosion. Some councils are considering managed retreat, gradually moving infrastructure away from vulnerable areas. Such decisions are controversial, as they affect property values, cultural connections to place and the identity of entire towns.

Effective disaster warnings depend on more than accurate forecasts. People must receive the warning, understand it and believe it applies to them. Research shows that warnings which state clearly what people should do are more effective than those that only describe the hazard. Language, technology access and past experience all influence how communities respond. For this reason, emergency agencies increasingly work with local groups to tailor messages to different audiences.
